issues.legal_issue: Statutory interest is unavailable for a period of possession that preceded publication of the preliminary acquisition notification.
material_facts: The claimant was dispossessed before the later acquisition proceedings began.
The earlier acquisition proceedings were declared invalid by a decree that became final.
The Collector’s later award included statutory interest running from the earlier dispossession, and the High Court set that interest aside.
issues.conclusion: The claimant was not entitled to interest under the acquisition statute for the period before publication of the preliminary notification; the High Court was correct to set aside that part of the award.
issues.legal_principle: Section 34 must be read in the context of the Act’s acquisition and possession provisions: the possession that triggers statutory interest is possession taken lawfully under Sections 16 or 17, after the required acquisition steps. Possession before publication of a Section 4(1) notification is de hors the Act and cannot trigger interest under Section 34; the same understanding of lawful possession informs Section 28. Union of India v. Budh Singh and Smt. Lila Ghosh v. State of West Bengal support this conclusion. Shri Vijay Cotton & Oil Mills v. State of Gujarat did not decide whether statutory interest is payable for pre-notification possession and is not authority for that proposition; the Court also relies on the principle that a decision is authority for what it actually decides, as stated in Krishena Kumar v. Union of India, Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Gurnam Kaur, and M/s. Orient Paper and Industries Ltd. v. State of Orissa.

predicates.possession_preceded_acquisition_notice: The state took possession before publication of the preliminary notice that began the acquisition proceedings.

issues.definition: When a land-acquisition compensation proceeding concerns possession taken before the preliminary acquisition notice, statutory interest is excluded for that earlier period.

issues.legal_issue: The additional statutory amount on market value is unavailable for a period before publication of the preliminary acquisition notification.
material_facts: The claimant was dispossessed before the later acquisition proceedings began.
The Collector’s later award included an additional amount calculated from the earlier dispossession.
The Court considered conflicting decisions on whether that additional amount could cover a pre-notification period.
issues.conclusion: The claimant was not entitled to the additional statutory amount for the period before publication of the preliminary notification; the contrary view in Assistant Commissioner, Gadag, Sub-Division, Gadag v. Mathapathi Basavanewwa was overruled.
issues.legal_principle: Section 23(1-A) ties the additional amount to a period beginning on publication of the notification under Section 4(1). The Court followed Special Tehsildar (LA) PWD Schemes Vijaywada v. M.A. Jabbar and held that the additional amount does not extend to a period before that publication; it rejected the contrary holding in Assistant Commissioner, Gadag, Sub-Division, Gadag v. Mathapathi Basavanewwa.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding: The proceeding determines compensation for land acquired by the state.
predicates.possession_preceded_acquisition_notice: The state took possession before publication of the preliminary notice that began the acquisition proceedings.

issues.definition: When possession in a land-acquisition compensation proceeding precedes the preliminary acquisition notice, the additional statutory amount is excluded for the earlier period.

issues.legal_issue: Pre-notification dispossession may support a claim for rent or damages for use and occupation, but the claimant was not entitled to an additional equitable payment for that period on these facts.
material_facts: The state took possession before the later acquisition proceedings, while title remained with the owner, who could have sought recovery of possession.
The claimant had received and retained compensation under the earlier award, which was almost twice the price he had paid for the land.
The earlier acquisition proceedings were declared invalid, and a fresh acquisition was later undertaken.
The later award compensated the claimant for the land and included solatium.
issues.conclusion: For pre-notification possession, the owner’s remedy is rent or damages for use and occupation, rather than statutory interest under the acquisition statute; the Collector may determine that amount when determining later compensation and may award appropriate interest for delayed payment. However, the claimant was not entitled to a further amount for the period in question on equitable grounds.
issues.legal_principle: Before lawful acquisition, title remains with the owner and the owner may pursue recovery of possession or claim rent or damages for use and occupation. The Court considered Section 48 as supporting the possibility that the Collector may determine such rent or damages while determining compensation, with appropriate interest at the prevailing bank rate for delayed payment. Applying equitable considerations, it also relied on the claimant’s retention of earlier compensation that was almost twice the purchase price and the compensation and solatium awarded in the later acquisition.
